Mixture-of-experts inference assigns each token to a learned subset of expert FFN layers via a routing function — typically a top-k softmax gating — but the central problem is that this routing is input-conditional and non-uniform: some experts attract disproportionate token flow while others sit idle, and this imbalance is not random noise but a learned, self-reinforcing attractor state driven by the training dynamics of auxiliary load-balancing losses that are often too weak to fully counteract preference collapse. The expert worries not about average-case throughput but about tail latency under heterogeneous batching: when a batch mixes long-document and short-query requests, routing distributions diverge sharply across sequence positions, causing specific experts to become bottlenecks that hold up the entire batch's decode step while underloaded experts waste compute capacity. Load imbalance entrenchment refers to the phenomenon — documented in Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2022) and later in Mixtral analyses — where experts that receive more tokens during training develop stronger weights, which attract even more tokens at inference, creating a routing feedback loop that baking-in structural hot spots that resist post-hoc correction. What beginners miss is that expert capacity buffers (the fixed token-slot ceiling per expert per forward pass) convert this soft statistical imbalance into a hard computational discontinuity: tokens overflowing capacity are either dropped or rerouted, introducing output quality degradation that is invisible in perplexity aggregates but surfaces as anomalous failures on specific input distributions. The throughput variance problem compounds because GPU kernel efficiency is highly sensitive to expert load uniformity — a perfectly balanced MoE batch achieves near-linear scaling, while an imbalanced one causes warp divergence and memory bandwidth waste that can degrade effective throughput by 30–50% on realistic serving workloads (as measured in DeepSpeed-MoE, Rajbhandari et al., 2022).

When expert capacity overflow occurs, the standard implementation choice — used in Switch Transformer and GShard (Lepikhin et al., 2021) — is to pass the overflowed token's representation unchanged through the residual connection, effectively treating the expert sublayer as an identity function for that token at that layer. This means the token's residual stream receives no expert-mediated transformation: no nonlinear projection, no expert-specific feature extraction, just the raw pre-gate representation forwarded directly to the layer norm and next attention block. The downstream consequence is insidious: the next layer's router receives a representation that is systematically shallower than representations of non-overflowed tokens at the same sequence position, because it missed a transformation step that all other tokens received, yet the router has no signal indicating this — it treats all incoming representations as equally valid routing inputs. Empirically, Zhou et al. (2022) in "Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing" showed that under standard top-k token-choice routing, overflow rates on natural language benchmarks can reach 10–20% of tokens per layer in hot experts, meaning a non-trivial fraction of the batch is accumulating representation debt across multiple layers if the same experts are overloaded repeatedly. This creates a routing pathology cascade: because overflowed tokens are shallower, their next-layer gate logits are distorted in a correlated way — they tend to route toward whatever expert their degraded representation points to, which may differ from where a fully-transformed representation would route, introducing systematic divergence between intended and actual expert assignment across the depth of the network. ST-MoE (Zoph et al., 2022) partially addressed this with router z-loss regularization to stabilize gate logits, but this operates on the routing distribution rather than repairing the representation deficit itself, meaning the fundamental residual stream corruption under overflow remains unaddressed in most deployed systems.

Yes, and the mechanism is more precise than it might first appear: tokens competing for the same hot expert share semantic similarity by construction (that's why the router sent them there), so overflow selectively degrades a semantically coherent subset of the token population — for instance, all entity mentions, all numeric tokens, or all domain-specific terminology in a technical document — rather than a random sample, meaning the representation shallowness is not noise but structured omission along feature dimensions that the hot expert specialized in. When these degraded tokens enter the next attention layer, their key and query projections are computed from corrupted representations, so the attention logits they produce are systematically deflated or misdirected relative to their true semantic role — effectively, the attention mechanism sees a population of tokens that have been made to look more similar to each other and less discriminable from background context tokens, because the expert transformation that would have sharpened their features was skipped. This matters acutely for tasks like coreference resolution, named entity disambiguation, and cross-sentence numerical reasoning, where the model must attend sharply to specific token identities; Park et al. (2024) in work on MoE faithfulness found that expert routing failures correlate with degraded entity tracking across long contexts, consistent with this mechanism. The problem compounds because attention is quadratic in token interaction: a degraded key vector doesn't just hurt that token's own retrieval, it corrupts the attention distribution for every query token in the sequence that would have relied on it, propagating the representation deficit laterally across the full context window. In heterogeneous batches, this effect is request-type-dependent — a long-document summarization request with dense entity fields will suffer far more structured attention bias than a short factual query with sparse entity load, which means throughput variance and quality variance are coupled in a way that standard perplexity or latency benchmarks completely obscure. Notably, Expert Choice routing (Zhou et al., 2022) inverts the selection direction (experts pick tokens rather than tokens picking experts) and eliminates overflow by design, but introduces its own attention bias problem: tokens not selected by any expert in a layer receive the identity pass-through systematically, and these unselected tokens tend to cluster in semantically predictable ways, recreating the structured omission problem under a different selection regime.

The honest answer is that structured omission is essentially inevitable under any fixed-capacity routing regime, and the reason is information-theoretic rather than implementation-specific: if total expert compute per layer is bounded (capacity factor C × number of experts × tokens/expert), then any input distribution with non-uniform routing preferences must either drop tokens, dilute expert specialization, or serialize computation — there is no fourth option that preserves both full coverage and expert distinctiveness at fixed cost. THOR (Zuo et al., 2022) and hash-based routing (Roller et al., 2021) attempt to escape this by making routing input-independent — assigning tokens to experts deterministically by position or hash — which guarantees perfect load balance and zero overflow, but at the cost of destroying the learned specialization that makes MoE useful in the first place, trading structured omission for structured irrelevance. The most principled near-escape is soft MoE (Puigcerver et al., 2023, Google DeepMind), which replaces discrete token-to-expert assignment with a differentiable weighted combination: each expert receives a soft mixture of all tokens, weighted by routing scores, and returns a weighted combination back to the residual stream — this eliminates hard overflow entirely and ensures every token receives some transformation from every expert. However, soft MoE's coverage guarantee comes with a representational cost: the per-expert input is now a centroid of the token distribution rather than individual token representations, which means fine-grained token-level distinctions are smoothed before the expert even processes them — exchanging post-hoc omission for pre-hoc averaging, which is arguably worse for token discrimination tasks. The capacity-specialization tradeoff has a formal analog in rate-distortion theory: achieving zero representation degradation requires either infinite expert capacity (trivially, dense computation) or zero expert specialization (uniform routing), and any point between these extremes accepts some distortion — what varies across routing schemes is only the structure of that distortion, not its existence. Empirically, soft MoE outperforms hard-routing MoE on image classification benchmarks (Puigcerver et al. report +1.5–2% on ImageNet at matched FLOP budgets) but has seen limited adoption in language modeling at scale, partly because the all-to-all soft aggregation step is communication-expensive in distributed inference and partly because the pre-hoc averaging interacts poorly with autoregressive generation where individual token identity is critical.

In single-token decoding the within-layer capacity overflow problem does vanish — one token cannot exceed any expert's capacity buffer — but the load imbalance problem transforms rather than disappears, shifting from a spatial (within-batch) phenomenon to a temporal (across-generation-steps) one: the router makes a fresh expert assignment at every decode step, and these assignments are not independent draws but correlated sequences driven by the evolving hidden state, meaning certain experts get visited repeatedly across a generation trajectory while others are rarely or never consulted for a given request. This temporal routing concentration has been characterized in the Mixtral inference literature as expert activation locality: for a given prompt type and generation context, empirical routing traces show that roughly 20-30% of experts account for 70-80% of token assignments across the full generation, with the active expert subset remaining surprisingly stable across consecutive decode steps — this is not random exploration of expert space but a quasi-deterministic trajectory through a small expert neighborhood. The serving-level imbalance pathology that emerges is cross-request expert contention: in a batched decode serving scenario (continuous batching, as in vLLM), multiple concurrent requests each pull toward their own expert subsets, and requests with similar prompt distributions cluster their routing onto the same experts simultaneously, creating hot experts at the system level even though no single request exceeds per-request capacity. This is qualitatively different from prefill-phase imbalance and harder to mitigate: prefill imbalance can be addressed with expert parallelism and careful batch packing, but decode-phase contention is dynamic and unpredictable because it depends on the joint routing trajectory of all concurrently active requests, which evolves with each generation step. Rajbhandari et al. (2022) in DeepSpeed-MoE measured that decode-phase expert utilization variance across a heterogeneous serving workload was 3-4× higher than prefill-phase variance, directly translating to memory bandwidth waste on underutilized expert weight matrices that must nonetheless remain resident on-device. A further pathology is routing trajectory rigidity: because the decode-phase router conditions on a hidden state that was shaped by all prior routing decisions in that generation, early routing choices constrain later ones — a token routed suboptimally in layer 3 of step 5 produces a degraded representation that biases routing in layer 3 of step 6, creating a form of routing hysteresis that has no analog in prefill processing where all positions are processed simultaneously and routing errors don't propagate temporally.

The quasi-determinism of decode routing trajectories does make prefix-conditioned routing prediction theoretically attractive, and there is concrete evidence it works in narrow regimes: Zheng et al. (2023) in "Pit: Optimization of Dynamic Sparse Deep Learning Models" and related work on MoE serving show that routing decisions for the first 10-20 decode steps are predictable from prefill routing statistics with ~75-85% accuracy for same-domain requests, sufficient to pre-load predicted expert weights into faster memory tiers before they are needed. The practical implementation is a speculative routing cache: after prefill, the system records the expert activation pattern from the final prefill layers, uses this as a routing fingerprint to retrieve a predicted decode trajectory from a lookup table built offline over representative prompts, and pre-fetches the predicted expert weights from CPU/NVMe into GPU HBM ahead of the actual routing decision — effectively hiding the memory latency of expert weight loading behind computation. The first major failure mode is trajectory divergence on generative branching: routing predictions trained on deterministic or greedy trajectories fail when sampling introduces token-level randomness, because a single unexpected high-probability token early in generation can shift the hidden state into a different expert neighborhood, causing all subsequent pre-fetched weights to be wrong and the pre-fetch overhead to become pure waste rather than latency savings. The second failure mode is domain shift within a single generation: long-form generations that transition across topics (e.g., a response that starts with code and transitions to prose explanation) exhibit routing regime changes mid-trajectory that no prefix-conditioned predictor can anticipate, because the prefix fingerprint captures only the initial domain signature and the transition point is content-dependent. A subtler third failure mode concerns self-fulfilling routing artifacts: if the system pre-loads predicted experts and the routing decision is made under memory pressure that causes non-predicted experts to be evicted, the actual routing may be implicitly biased toward predicted experts simply because they are available at lower latency — the prediction system then corrupts the routing distribution it was meant to passively observe, making offline trajectory statistics unreliable for future prediction calibration. Quantitatively, the break-even point for speculative routing is tight: pre-fetching expert weights for a Mixtral 8x7B layer requires moving ~200MB per expert prediction, and if trajectory prediction accuracy drops below ~60-65%, the bandwidth cost of wrong pre-fetches exceeds the latency saved by correct ones, meaning the optimization regime is narrow and highly sensitive to workload distribution shift.

Real-time regime change detection is feasible in principle and the most natural signal is the router's own gate logit entropy: during stable routing trajectories, the top-k gate logits are sharply peaked (low entropy, confident expert selection), while regime transitions produce transient entropy spikes as the hidden state moves between expert neighborhoods — monitoring per-layer gate entropy with an exponential moving average and flagging deviations beyond 1.5-2σ provides a lightweight detector that adds negligible compute overhead since the gate logits are already computed. This entropy-based detector has a concrete analog in the language modeling literature: Xue et al. (2024) in MoE-I2 observe that routing entropy correlates strongly with semantic boundary events in long-form generation, validating the intuition that topic transitions and domain shifts manifest as measurable instability in the routing distribution before they fully propagate into the residual stream. The harder problem is what to do upon detection: naive adaptive re-routing — resetting expert assignments or injecting auxiliary load-balancing loss signals mid-generation — breaks the autoregressive invariant that each token's representation must be a deterministic function of prior context, because changing the routing function mid-trajectory means the model being used for step N+1 is effectively a different model than the one used for steps 1 through N, introducing representational discontinuities that corrupt the KV cache's implicit assumptions. A principled partial escape is layer-wise routing reset with KV cache invalidation: upon detecting a regime change at step T, selectively invalidate and recompute KV cache entries for the layers where routing entropy spiked, accepting the recompute cost in exchange for representational consistency — but this is expensive (potentially re-running attention over the full context) and reintroduces exactly the throughput variance problem that motivated the prediction system in the first place. The load imbalance reintroduction risk is real but asymmetric: regime change events are rare (empirically, major domain shifts occur in perhaps 5-15% of decode steps in mixed long-form generation), so an adaptive system that accepts rebalancing overhead only at detected transition points imposes far lower average cost than continuous dynamic load balancing, provided the detector's false positive rate is kept below ~5% to avoid spurious cache invalidations. The deepest tension here is that the detector and the predictor are in conflict: a high-sensitivity entropy detector will trigger re-routing frequently, undermining the stability that makes routing prediction accurate, while a low-sensitivity detector misses genuine regime changes and allows representational drift to compound — suggesting the optimal operating point requires joint calibration of detector threshold and prediction confidence that is workload-specific and cannot be set universally.

Partial KV cache invalidation after a routing regime change does not restore representational consistency — it creates a routing-regime chimera in the cache: entries computed under the pre-transition routing regime and entries recomputed under the post-transition regime coexist in the same cache, and the attention mechanism has no mechanism to distinguish them, treating all cached key-value pairs as if they were produced by a single coherent forward pass. The violation is more fundamental than typical cache staleness problems because routing regime differences affect representations multiplicatively through layer composition: a key vector at layer L encodes transformations applied at layers 1 through L-1, so a cache entry from the old regime at layer 8 reflects a different sequence of expert projections than a freshly computed entry at layer 8, and when attention at layer 9 mixes these two populations, the resulting context vector is a linear combination of representations from incompatible computational histories. Concretely, in a Mixtral-class model where each token passes through 2 of 8 experts per layer across 32 layers, two tokens processed under different routing regimes have potentially diverged at every layer — the representational distance between old-regime and new-regime cache entries is not a small perturbation but can span the full inter-expert representational gap, which Dai et al. (2024) in work on MoE representation geometry estimate at 0.3-0.6 cosine distance units for domain-shifted inputs, far exceeding the noise tolerance of typical attention softmax distributions. The attention softmax compounds the problem through its normalization structure: when a query attends over a mixed cache containing high-magnitude old-regime keys and lower-magnitude new-regime keys (or vice versa), the softmax temperature is effectively distorted by the magnitude mismatch, causing the query to over-attend to whichever regime produced larger key norms — introducing a systematic attention bias that has nothing to do with semantic relevance and everything to do with the accident of which cache entries were invalidated. Full cache invalidation and recomputation from the regime change point forward would restore consistency but at O(T) cost for a generation of length T, which is prohibitive and eliminates any latency advantage of the KV cache entirely for long generations. The honest conclusion is that routing regime changes are not safely recoverable within a single generation under standard KV caching architecture: the cache coherence violation introduced by partial invalidation is arguably worse than accepting the representational drift from the original regime change, because drift accumulates gradually while chimera caches introduce discontinuous attention distortions — suggesting that the correct system response to a detected regime change may be to terminate and restart generation rather than attempt mid-flight repair.
